title: Bayes in a minute
objectives: Solve interview Bayes questions quickly with natural frequencies.

screens.title: Count people, not percentages
screens.prose: A disease affects 1% of people. A test catches 99% of those who have it, and wrongly flags 5% of those who do not. Picture 10,000 people.

state.caption: A 1% base rate, a test that catches 99% of the ill, and 5% false positives.

screens.question: Fill in the two counts of positive tests.

hints.text: Take each percentage of its own group.
Ill and positive is 99% of the 100 ill people.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply each test rate to its own group, not to 10,000.

explain.text: The ill give $0.99 \times 100 = 99$ positives. The well give $0.05 \times 9{,}900 = 495$. These are **natural frequencies**: whole people instead of chances.

screens.title: Positive: how likely ill?
screens.prose: Someone tests positive. They are one of the $99 + 495 = 594$ positives on the tree.

state.caption: Every positive is one of the 99 or one of the 495.

screens.question: What is the chance they are ill? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the ill positives by all the positives.

byKey.accuracy: You quoted the test’s accuracy. Most positives come from the far larger well group.
byKey.ratio: You divided 99 by 495. Divide by all 594 positives, which include the 99.
byKey.base: That is the chance before the test. A positive raises it.

explain.text: Of 594 positives only 99 are ill, so the chance is $\tfrac16$. The 5% false positives fall on 9,900 people, which swamps the 99. Counting makes the base rate impossible to forget.

screens.title: The witness
screens.prose: In a town 15% of cars are blue and 85% green. A witness names a car’s colour correctly 80% of the time. Picture 100 cars.

state.caption: Blue dots: blue cars called blue (12). Yellow: blue cars called green (3). Orange: green cars called blue (17). Green: green cars called green (68).

screens.question: Tap every group the witness would call blue.

hints.text: A wrong call on a green car says blue.
The witness calls 12 blue cars blue.
Blue called blue, and green called blue.

feedback.correct: 12 blue cars and 17 green cars are called blue.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find every car the witness says is blue, right or wrong.

byKey.blue-cars: You tapped the blue cars. The question is what the witness says, and 17 green cars are called blue too.

explain.text: Blue cars called blue: 80% of 15, so 12. Green cars called blue: 20% of 85, so 17. In all, 29 cars are called blue.

canvas.caption: Called blue: the 12 blue dots and the 17 orange dots, 29 cars in all.

screens.title: Is it blue?
screens.prose: The witness says the car was blue. It is one of the 29 cars called blue.

state.caption: Blue dots: blue cars called blue (12). Yellow: blue cars called green (3). Orange: green cars called blue (17). Green: green cars called green (68).

screens.question: What is the chance it really was blue? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Only the cars called blue matter.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the blue cars called blue by all cars called blue.

byKey.witness: You quoted the witness’s accuracy. Green cars are so common that their mistakes outnumber the true calls.
byKey.base: That ignores what the witness said.
byKey.twelve: You divided by 100 cars. Divide by the 29 called blue.

explain.text: The witness calls 29 cars blue, and 12 of them are. So the chance is $\tfrac{12}{29} \approx 0.41$. A good witness still loses to a low base rate.

canvas.caption: Of the 29 cars called blue, 12 (the blue dots) are blue.

screens.title: Ten heads
screens.prose: A bag holds 1,000 coins. One has two heads, the rest are fair. You draw one and flip it ten times: ten heads.

state.caption: Draw a coin 1,024,000 times over, and flip it ten times each time.

screens.question: What is the chance you hold the two-headed coin? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Pick a count where every number is whole.
Over 1,024,000 draws, the two-headed coin comes up 1,024 times.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{1024}{2023} \approx 0.5062$, barely better than a coin toss.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the ten-head runs from each kind of coin.

byKey.base: You kept the chance before the flips. Ten heads is strong evidence.
byKey.sure: Fair coins also give ten heads, $\tfrac1{1024}$ of the time, and there are 999 of them.

explain.text: Choose a total that makes every count whole: $1{,}024{,}000$ draws. The rare coin gives 1,024 runs of ten heads and the fair coins 999. So the chance is $\tfrac{1024}{2023}$, about even.

screens.title: Quote the accuracy?
screens.prose: An interviewer says: a disease hits 1 in 500 people. A test is right 99% of the time, ill or well. You test positive.
screens.question: What do you say, roughly?

options.why: That is the blurted answer. Out of 100,000 people, 198 ill and 998 well test positive, so most positives are false.
You split the positives evenly. The well group is about 500 times larger, so its 1% errors dominate.
You ignored the test. A positive does move the chance up, about 80-fold.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the positives in each group of 100,000 people.

byKey.b: You quoted the accuracy. The question is about people who tested positive, and most of them are well.

explain.text: Of 100,000 people, 200 are ill and 198 test positive. Of the 99,800 well, 998 test positive. So a positive means ill with chance $198/1196 \approx 17\%$.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
Every answer came from counting. Pick a round total, split it by the base rate, then by the test rates. Divide the true positives by all positives:

$$P(\text{ill} \mid +) = \frac{\text{ill and } +}{\text{ill and } + \;+\; \text{well and } +}.$$
screens.question: Which total makes the 1% disease example cleanest?

options.why: One ill person would give 0.99 of a positive. Pick a total where every count is whole.
Chances of one person put you back in percentages. Counts are what make it fast.

feedback.correct: 10,000 gives 100 ill, 99 true positives and 495 false ones.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick a total where every count is a whole number.

explain.text: $1\%$ of $99\%$ needs four zeros to come out whole. With 10,000 the counts are 99 and 495.

screens.title: Odds in one line
screens.prose: For repeated tests an odds form is faster. Derive it from the counts of the first example.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Before the test: 100 ill to 9,900 well, so the prior odds are $1 : 99$.
The ill test positive at rate 0.99 and the well at 0.05: a likelihood ratio of $0.99/0.05 = 19.8$.
Positives: $100 \times 0.99$ to $9{,}900 \times 0.05$, which is the prior odds times the ratio.
So the posterior odds are $\tfrac1{99} \times 19.8 = \tfrac15$, a chance of $\tfrac16$.
Add the ratio to the prior odds: $\tfrac1{99} + 19.8$.

hints.text: Each group is scaled by its own test rate.
Prior odds, ratio, scaled counts, posterior odds.

feedback.correct: Posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the two ingredients, then scale the counts.

byKey.d1: Odds multiply. Each group’s count is scaled by its rate, so the ratio multiplies the odds.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the sum belongs.

explain.text: Each count is scaled by its own rate, so the odds are scaled by the ratio of the rates. Odds of $1 : 5$ mean a chance of $\tfrac16$. A second test multiplies by 19.8 again, if the tests err independently.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three new puzzles at about 3 minutes each, 9 in all. Keep your own time. Give each answer to four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: Monty Hall: you pick a door, the host opens a goat door. Chance you win by switching?
A signal fires on 60% of good days and 30% of bad days. 40% of days are good. Chance a day is good, given it fired?
The first disease test, given twice. Both positive, errors independent. Chance ill?

hints.text: Count for each: 3 doors, 100 days, 1,000,000 people.
Signal: 24 good days fire and 18 bad days fire.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Check Monty Hall. Your first pick wins $\tfrac13$ of the time, so switching wins $\tfrac23$.
byKey.r1c1: Check the signal. Out of 100 days, 24 good days fire and 18 bad days fire.
byKey.r2c1: Check the two tests. Out of 1,000,000 people, 9,801 ill and 2,475 well test positive twice.

explain.text: Switching wins whenever your first pick was wrong, $\tfrac23$. The signal: $\tfrac{24}{24 + 18} = \tfrac47$. Two tests: $\tfrac{9801}{9801 + 2475} \approx 0.7984$, since $0.99^2$ of 10,000 ill and $0.05^2$ of 990,000 well test positive twice.

screens.title: Follow-up: a third test
screens.prose: You said 0.7984 after two positives. The interviewer asks: and after a third positive? Use odds, and say what you assume.
screens.question: What is the chance of illness after three positive tests? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Each test multiplies the odds by 19.8.

feedback.correct: Odds of about $78.4 : 1$, a chance of $0.9874$, if the tests err independently.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the prior odds by 19.8 three times, then turn odds into a chance.

byKey.odds: That is the odds. Convert: chance $= \tfrac{\text{odds}}{1 + \text{odds}}$.
byKey.accuracy: You quoted the test again. Three tests make it close to that, but not equal.

explain.text: The odds go from $\tfrac1{99}$ to $\tfrac{19.8^3}{99} \approx 78.41$, so the chance is $78.41/79.41 \approx 0.9874$. Say the assumption aloud: the errors are independent. Repeating one faulty test on one sample would break it.

screens.title: A crash alert
screens.prose: A model alerts before 90% of market crashes, which hit 2% of days. It also fires on 10% of calm days. Picture 1,000 trading days.

state.caption: Orange: crash days with an alert (18). Yellow: crash days without (2). Blue: calm days with an alert (98). Green: calm days without (882).

screens.question: The alert fires today. What is the chance a crash follows? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Count the alert days of each kind.
18 crash days and 98 calm days have an alert.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide crash alerts by all alerts.

byKey.hit: You quoted the hit rate. Calm days are 49 times as common, so their 10% false alerts swamp the true ones.
byKey.ratio: You divided 18 by 98. Divide by all 116 alerts.

explain.text: Of 1,000 days, 18 crash days and 98 calm days carry an alert. So an alert means a crash with chance $\tfrac{18}{116} \approx 16\%$. A high hit rate on a rare event still gives mostly false alarms.

canvas.caption: Alert days: 18 orange (crash) and 98 blue (calm), 116 in all.

ideas: Pick a round total that makes every count whole, then split by the base rate and the test rates.
The answer is the true positives over all positives.
For repeated independent tests, multiply the prior odds by the likelihood ratio each time.

formula.name: Odds form
formula.note: $L$ is the likelihood ratio. The 1% test: $\tfrac1{99} \times 19.8 = \tfrac15$, a chance of $\tfrac16$.

summary.trap: Quoting the test’s accuracy, 99%, as the answer. A rare condition makes most positives false.

quiz.prose: One email in five is spam. A filter flags 90% of spam and 2% of good emails.
quiz.question: What is the chance a flagged email is spam? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: Out of 1,000 emails: 180 spam and 16 good are flagged, so $\tfrac{180}{196} \approx 0.9184$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count flagged emails of each kind out of 1,000.

byKey.hit: You quoted the filter’s hit rate. Divide flagged spam by all flagged emails.

explain.text: Out of 1,000: 200 spam give 180 flags, and 800 good give 16. Here the base rate is high, so a flag is usually right.

quiz.prose: Return to the 1% disease and the test that catches 99%. Its false positive rate is cut from 5% to 2.5%.
quiz.question: Now what is the chance a positive is ill? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recount the false positives out of 10,000.

byKey.double: You doubled the old answer. Halving the false positives does not double the chance, because the true positives stay in the bottom line.
byKey.old: That is the answer with 5% false positives.

explain.text: False positives fall to $0.025 \times 9{,}900 = 247.5$. So the chance is $99/346.5 = \tfrac27$. In odds: the ratio doubles from 19.8 to 39.6, so the odds double to $\tfrac25$.

quiz.prose: A test never flags a well person: its false positive rate is 0. It catches 70% of the ill.
quiz.question: You test positive. What is the chance you are ill?

options.why: That is the chance an ill person tests positive. With no false positives, every positive is ill.

options.text: It depends on the base rate
options.why: The base rate sets how many positives there are, but none of them can be well.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the well people who test positive.

explain.text: With no false positives the bottom line holds only true positives. The edge case shows why false positives drive these answers.
